title: Debugging Go Cache Invalidation Logic
scenario: A security engineer is auditing a small Go-based in-house service that caches frequently accessed user data. The service uses a custom, in-memory cache with an expiry mechanism, intended to reduce database load and improve response times. Recently, users have reported seeing stale data, indicating a potential issue with the cache invalidation or expiry logic.
instruction_draft: Our in-house user data service has a custom in-memory cache that is experiencing stale data issues. We need you to fix the cache invalidation logic so that user data is consistently up-to-date. The service must also meet a performance target for cache lookups and invalidations.
requirements: The service must correctly invalidate cached user data when it is updated.
The service must correctly expire stale user data based on its TTL.
environment: A small Go codebase (approx. 1000 lines) for a user data service.
Includes a `main.go` entrypoint, `user_data.go` (simulates DB access), and `cache.go` (custom in-memory cache implementation).
The `cache.go` file contains a subtle bug in its eviction or update logic, potentially related to concurrent access or incorrect TTL handling.
A small set of `protobuf` definitions for user data.
A small Go test suite that passes basic functionality but fails to catch the subtle bug.
A `test_server.go` utility to simulate client requests and measure performance.
internal_hint: The core issue lies within `cache.go`. The cache uses a map to store user data, keyed by user ID. It also maintains a separate mechanism for tracking expiry, possibly a time-based eviction queue or similar. The bug could stem from: 1. Incorrect handling of concurrent updates to the same user's data, leading to race conditions where an older value overwrites a newer one after an update. 2. A flaw in the TTL calculation or expiry check, where items are not being marked for eviction or are being evicted prematurely/late. 3. An issue with the eviction strategy itself, perhaps not correctly removing items from the underlying map when their TTL expires. The performance threshold requires an efficient cache implementation, so simply increasing memory or using a less optimized approach will fail.
trap: A naive solution might focus solely on fixing the apparent stale data by ensuring updates write the latest value. However, if the underlying concurrency or expiry logic is not robust, the solution will still fail under heavy load or specific timing conditions. A solution that passes the basic functional tests but doesn't address the performance requirement will also fail. For instance, a solution that adds excessive locking or uses a less efficient data structure for expiry tracking might fix the staleness but exceed the latency thresholds.
tests: Test 2: Cache update and subsequent hit with new data.
Test 3: Cache expiry – data is stale after TTL.
Test 4: Concurrent updates to multiple users – no stale data, correct values.
Test 5: Concurrent updates and reads to the *same* user – no stale data, correct values.
Test 6: High load test simulating many concurrent requests to stress the cache's concurrency handling and expiry.
Test 7: Performance test measuring average cache lookup latency under load.
Test 8: Performance test measuring average cache update/invalidation latency under load.
Test 9: A specific scenario designed to trigger a race condition in cache update/expiry.
Test 10: A scenario involving rapid TTL expirations and subsequent lookups.

verifier_knob.name: number_of_request_scenarios
verifier_knob.effect: Increasing this number adds more complex concurrent request patterns and edge cases for cache expiry and updates, making it harder to pass all tests without a robust solution.

expected_failure_modes: Race conditions in concurrent cache updates or evictions.
Performance degradation due to overly aggressive locking or inefficient data structures.
Failure to handle edge cases in cache expiry under high load.
Incorrect assumptions about the cache's internal data structures leading to subtle bugs.
